utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. On this Thursday I would like to say good morning to all those present in the courtroom, the Prosecution, the Defence, and the members of the registry who are assisting us in our proceedings. I take that Mr. Stojic isn't here today, but I think he has a medical check-up. He will be represented by his counsel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, that's correct. There's no problem with proceeding in Mr. Stojic's absence today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have a witness who is going to be introduced into court, but before that could the registrar read out the IC numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness A. The list submitted by OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 412. The list submitted by 2D shall be given exhibit number 413. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 414. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit number IC 415. The OTP has submitted a list of objections to 2D's list of documents tendered through Witness A. That shall be given IC 416. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am now going to read an oral decision having to do with documents tendered through Witness CY, who appeared in 29 January 2007. The Chamber has ruled to admit P 08489 under seal. It is 08486, under seal. The document was tendered by the Prosecution through the list IC 00266 on the grounds that the document represents probative value and a certain relevance. Furthermore, the Chamber has decided to admit Exhibit 4D 00489 under seal, tendered by the Petkovic Defence team, based on list IC 00267, on the grounds that the document has certain probative value and certain relevance. This decision was a unanimous decision made by the Judges. We're now going to have the witness shown in. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness does come in, I would like to go on record with respect to what we received yesterday as part of the proofing notes, because I think it's rather important. As you well know, Your Honour -- Your Honours, we were provided with the gentleman's statement. We were also provided with the -- with the summary. Of course we understand that the summary is just that, what they expected the witness to testify to and there must be some flexibility as to what the witness will actually testify to and as to what counts of the indictment the testimony would go to, so we -- I say that with the full understanding that we cannot expect the Prosecution to be absolutely perfect on each and every occasion as to what each and every witness will testify to. However, yesterday afternoon we receive what amounts to proofing notes, but it's not just proofing notes. The scope of the testimony now is drastically different. There is -- the information that the witness intends to testify to is significantly more than what it was intended. Now, why is that a problem? Because we're in the middle of a trial. Normally what our practice is, is do our own investigation as part of our own preparation for each and every witness. It becomes virtually impossible at times to do extensive research in the middle of a trial in a late afternoon when the next day the witness is about to appear. Now, in light of the topics that the gentleman wishes to testify to, all of which, all of which are -- seem to be new to us today, I think it's only fair that the cross-examination be delayed. The gentleman is here. We'll hear his direct, but I think a fair amount of time should be provided to the Defence in order to meaningfully prepare for cross-examination. We know that it's an inconvenience for the witness. It certainly is not -- the Prosecution is not being prejudiced, but at the same time, if cross-examination were to go on today and to -- for -- and for the entire testimony of this witness to take place today, I believe that it would amount to manifest injustice for all of the accused here in court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to say that I wholly support what my colleague Mr. Karnavas has said, and one of the new areas that the Prosecution has informed us that the witness will be testifying about, about the old bridge, was not mentioned at all in his original statement, and therefore we have not prepared for that area. But we consider it a very important area which is very controversial. We have a lot of evidence to the contrary, and we have -- the right to explore this area, so I fully endorse what Mr. Karnavas has already said. If the Prosecution is changing the scope and it certainly is because it's more than double. Then the only solution will be to bring the witness in, in due course, for the cross-examination or an additional cross-examination, and then we would ask for more time to be allotted to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is not going to deny that the witness yesterday in proofing gave a lot of new evidence that is not in his statement, in his written statement, and if indeed the Defence needs more time for cross-examination on these new elements, the Prosecution would not object for the witness to be cross-examined later on, on these topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as I'm concerned, I have taken note of what you have said, and this new element, the old bridge topic, it is quite true that the old bridge was not a topic that was mentioned at the beginning. So if the Prosecution has nothing against the requests made, then this will be the subject of cross-examination at some later date. But I'm very surprised, let me say, that the Defence, since we've been sitting for almost a year now, that the Defence is telling me now that it is not capable of cross-examining a witness on the topic of the old bridge at this point in the trial. It is absolutely amazing as far as I'm concerned. I have said that I have taken note of it, but I really can't understand why that is, because we have a commander of this unit in Donja Mahala. He is the witness. We know where Donja Mahala is. Even I myself, without knowing what he said in written form previously, there are some automatic questions that must be asked him without having specially prepared. So I'm stupefied. And to discover that you need time to prepare, well, maybe. I know that you have a lot of work to get through, a quite considerable work, in actual fact, but with your high professional level, which you have demonstrated on a number of occasions throughout these proceedings, I'm sure would have allowed you to broach the topic of the old bridge and to go to the heart of the matter and ask essential questions. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You who is a great professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Precisely because I believe in due diligence, Your Honour; that's the problem. Yes, I can stand up and, from the seat of my pants, as they say, conduct cross-examination. I want to be prepared. I want to be very thorough. There's a lot -- there's a lot more information, not just the bridge itself, but I want to be very thorough because I do represent Mr. Prlic who deserves to have the best possible trial, and I would be doing a disservice to Mr. Prlic if I just simply stood up and did a cross-examination half prepared, or even 80 per cent prepared. Mr. Prlic is not entitled to 50 per cent of due process, or 80 per cent of due process, or even 90 per cent of due process. He is entitled to 100 per cent of due process. I'm trying to give him that, and perhaps I'm not as good as you might be suggesting, but I do try to be as professional as possible, and I think my colleagues will share with me the fact that these sorts of new information, this sort of new information deserves to be looked at and checked at carefully. So I don't want to give the impression that we cannot do a cross, but it's not a proper cross. And if we're going to do it, let's do it right. And this is new information and -- and I'm just trying to be a professional, Mr. President. I'm not trying to delay the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. Just a moment, please. Perhaps we can find a solution. As far as the Prosecution is concerned, Mr. Bos, would the ideal thing be for you not to ask questions on the old bridge? Can you do that? Because as far as the old bridge is concerned there will be other witnesses. So is it really useful to broach the topic of the old bridge with this particular witness? Perhaps we could leave that out and do that with other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I would really like to have this witness to speak about the old bridge. This witness is -- actually was on the bridge on -- on the night of the 8th of November, and he saw, you know, the type of damage that was done on the bridge, which I think is important enough for this witness to -- to be heard on this. So -- but one of the solutions may be, Your Honours, that this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, within the 400 lists -- 400 witnesses that you have on the 65 ter list, is that really the only witness that you have to examine about the old bridge?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not saying that this is the only witness on the old bridge but I'm saying that's -- the evidence that he gave on the old bridge is important evidence and we want to hear that evidence. And, Your Honours, if I may have a suggestion. What we could do is have the examination-in-chief of this witness this morning and then have a cross-examination maybe on Monday. We can maybe adjust the schedule in such a way that we can have the cross-examination on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't agree on that score. Yes, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Without any desire to bring Mr. Kovacic and Mr. Karnavas in a difficult position with respect to their right to cross-examine and the procedure on the part of the Prosecution. As far as the old bridge is concerned, I can say that I stand ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I represent Mr. Prlic. I don't represent Mr. Praljak. Mr. Praljak may be ready, but I am not ready for my client, and I made it very clear. And I fully support the Prosecution that they should be able to present all of their evidence. And it's not just the bridge. It's about sniping, it's about sniping positions, there's all sorts of new information, and while Mr. Praljak may be ready, I am not and Mr. Prlic is represented by me. And unless Mr. Prlic is willing to waive his rights to a fair trial I don't believe that I should be going forward on behalf simply because one accused thinks that he is prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask Mr. Karnavas if -- if there was a cross-examination opportunity on Monday discussing the topic of the old bridge whether that would be acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe that would be an acceptable solution, Mr. President. That would give us at least sufficient time to have our investigator look into some of the matters that are being mentioned for the first time by this witness. I think that would be a reasonable amount of time. And I apologise for raising my voice, but I rarely, rarely ask for continuances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber has made an oral ruling and will grant the request made; the cross-examination, but just on the topic of the old bridge, will be held on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, no. We would like the entire cross-examination on Monday. Because, as I've indicated, he's talking about sniping positions for the very first time. He's talking about all sorts of things. It's not just the old bridge. Yes, he mentions the old bridge, but there are other things. This is a completely new statement. Radically new. That's my whole point, Mr. President. It's not just something that was in passing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to go round the table once again with the new elements -- as far as new elements and topics are concerned, I just see that being the old bridge, because Hum and the sniping incidents have been explained at length already. So fundamentally speaking, there's only the old bridge to address. That's a new topic. The -- let me turn to the Prosecution. Does the Prosecution feel that there are knew elements, new topics with respect to what was in the written statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as -- as Your Honour yourself just said, as far as the sniping is concerned, yes, there are a couple of new elements but we've been discussing sniping for, you know, for several weeks now. So if you compare to the evidence -- to the old bridge yes there is new evidence as far as sniping there are a couple of new elements but I wouldn't compare it in the way with -- with the evidence of the old bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. The sniping, of course we are all aware of the subject matter because we were dealing with that for couple of weeks, but this is the witness who was not mentioning nothing related to the sniping. So we have to go back and prepare for this witness. [Interpretation] I apologise for speaking in English. Perhaps it would be more proper in Croatian. But, Your Honours, I think that it would be a very reasonable solution and quite obviously the Prosecution is that way inclined, and we are ready, and my client has said that if he is ready -- if he needs to, he's ready today. But it's a question of all the technical elements and preparations and so on. So I think that would be a reasonable solution and a minimum loss of time, if the examination-in-chief were to be completed today and we start off with a normal cross-examination in its entirety at a later date. I would like to ask a little more time than would usually be accorded me for my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are a number of subjects the Chamber had to deliberate about. First of all, as to time. One hour 30 minutes is what the Prosecution has asked for, for the examination-in-chief on the sniping and the old bridge. But since we have new elements with respect to the written statement, the new topic being the old bridge, the Chamber gives one more hour to the Defence. So they will have 2 hours and 30 minutes. Having said that, the Prosecution will conduct the examination-in-chief today. Mr. Praljak's Defence have told us that they are capable of cross-examining on any military subject. We'll begin their cross-examination, and if the other Defence teams wish to participate before the end of the day they are -- they can do so, and then on Monday we'll take up the cross-examination for Mr. Prlic in its entirety. Mr. Prlic will conduct its entire cross-examination on Monday, and they will deal with the sniping as well as the topic of the old bridge. That is our ruling, and having said that, let us have the witness brought in. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to apologise to Mr. Karnavas. I wish to avoid any misunderstanding or meddling in anything else but to say that I am ready as far as the old bridge is concerned. It doesn't mean that Mr. Karnavas might be ready in his Defence case for Mr. Prlic. So I do apologise if I have made a faux pas in this courtroom and I'd like to apologise to Mr. Karnavas if that has been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And if I could just take this opportunity to make a clarification on the record that -- the impression was given that this witness in his statement doesn't talk about sniping, but that is incorrect. If you read paragraph 11 of his written statement, that deals with the witness -- snipers on Stotina and so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: To a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But not the extent of the proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The impression was given that there wasn't any evidence on sniping in his statement, and that's just what I want to make clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, let me see whether you are receiving the interpretation of my words in your own language. If so, please say yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you and I can understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, first of all, I would like you to take the solemn declaration. Could you give me your name, your family name, and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Miro Salcin, also known as Mira. I was born on the 9th of October, 1950 in Mostar at Donja Mahala at Gojka Vukovica Street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm the deputy of the commander of the firemen brigade's unit in the city's firemen brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have you ever testified before, before a local court or before an International Tribunal about the events that took place in your country in 1993 or is this the first time that you actually testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never testified about these events before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please lead -- read the text of the solemn declaration that the usher is giving to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. There are a few things that I need to tell you about your testimony. First of all, we had a procedural issue to deal with, and unfortunately you will have to stay until Monday. You will be taken care of by the Tribunal, and hopefully this will not cause any problems to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will stay for as long as you need me, and I can go back when I'm finished. I can go back any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's good news. Secondly, I would like to tell you that your examination is going to take place in the following way: First of all, you're going to answer questions put to you by the Prosecutors that you have already met with, and we have envisaged that the Prosecution will have an hour and a half at their disposal. During the examination-in-chief they will show you documents that you must have seen with the Prosecutors when they were proofing you. When that ends, the Defence teams, which are seated on your left, there are a number of Defence lawyers there, as well as the accused, will have an opportunity to put questions to you as well. The Chamber has given two hours and a half for their cross-examination. The Judges that are in front of you - usually there are four of us but today we are three - will also have questions to ask you. Between the three of us, the Prosecution, the Defence, and the Judges, when they put questions to you, try to be as precise as possible and up to the point, because we -- we are in the so-called oral procedure, and we have documents translated into English, and we also have the transcript that is in front of you on the screen. Everything you say will be recorded, so please be as precise as possible in your answers. Answer not quickly but, rather, slowly to allow the interpreters to interpret your words, because we are working in three languages and it takes time for the interpretation. If you do not understand the question, do not hesitate to ask the person who has put it to you to repeat it. If during the sitting at any point in time you feel a medical problem, please signal to us that that may be the case and we will stop the proceedings. This is in very general terms how your examination is going to take place today and on Monday. Having said this, I'm going to give the floor to the Prosecution. We have an hour before the break. Mr. Bos, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Salcin. Mr. Salcin, I'm first going to read out a rule 65 ter summary of your statement. The witness was a residents of Donja Mahala in Mostar. He was the commander of a company of men who were in charge of the defence of the Donja Mahala area. No humanitarian aid was received directly into Donja Mahala. They received their aid via a pulley system which they used to get aid across the Neretva River into Donja Mahala. In July 1993, the HVO began to fill tyres with explosives and rolled them down Mount Hum into the Donja Mahala area. Muslim detainees were used for forced labour and had to load the explosive-filled tyres onto trucks for the HVO. Detainees told the witness that Mladen Misic and a 4th HVO battalion were the ones responsible for rolling the tyres. They also dropped improvised bombs from a small aeroplane onto the East Mostar area. There was a day light curfew because of the danger of snipers who were indiscriminate as to who they targeted. Mr. Salcin, is it correct that you provided a statement to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 8th of July, 2005? You have to -- have to give an answer.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: The statement is correct and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And at the time that you provided this written statement, did you answer the questions of the investigator truthfully?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I swear by everything that I answered truthfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you answer the questions freely, without any coercion?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I answered all the questions freely, and I only spoke about things that I saw with my own two eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And at the conclusion of that interview, was your statement read back to you in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes, fully, and I also read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did you then sign the statement in the English language?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I signed both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If I could ask the usher now to provide this witness with a bundle of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness -- Witness, you've been provided with a bundle of documents, and I would like to ask you to look at the first document in this bundle, which is labelled 09834. Is this document a copy of the English statement, and does it bear your signature?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes. This is statement that I signed in the original, and now I have a copy of it before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yesterday when you met with myself and an investigator, you were -- were you given an opportunity to review your statement, and did you wanted to make any corrections to the statement? Is that -- maybe ...

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I just had one objection with regard to the shelling of Donja Mahala by the Serb army and the HVO. I stated at the time that 90 per cent of Mostar in Donja Mahala, in the local commune of Donja Mahala, was destroyed by the HVO and only 10 per cent were destroyed by the Serbs from their positions, and this is a true estimate which I stand by, and this would be the only correction to my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What you just stated, Witness, does that refer to paragraph 12 of your statement? Could you take a look at your own statement at paragraph 12. Is that the paragraph you've just been referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And if I could draw your attention to paragraph 8 of your statement. You have paragraph 8 in front of you? Is there anything you wanted to correct in paragraph 8 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: In paragraph 8 it says here that I was the company commander of Donja Mahala, and it doesn't mention that I was a captain and then assistant commander of another battalion in the sector from the old bridge to Cekrk. That would have been my formation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You've been referring to another battalion. Which battalion was this?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: This was the battalion that was on the right bank of the Neretva, and the Mahala company was just one part of the battalion, which had three companies all in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But what was the name of the battalion? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The true name of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Witness. The Prosecution asked you about the battalion, the -- in which you were an assistant command -- a commander. When you met up with the investigators of the Prosecution, and that meeting lasted for two or three days in 2005, the investigator didn't ask you to which battalion exactly you belonged. He didn't ask you to -- to explain the structure of the military unit that you belonged to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they didn't ask me about that. I don't -- I was never asked that before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the investigator first saw you, he knew that you were a member of the BiH army and he did not concern himself with what exactly you did? He didn't want know your rank or things like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Nobody asked me about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many hours did you spend talking to the investigator in July 2005?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not more than two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Bos, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, my question that I had put to you and you haven't given an answer yet, what was the name of this battalion?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: The true name of the battalion was the 2nd Battalion of the 441st Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, while you have your statement still in front of you, could I ask you to turn to -- to paragraph 11 of your statement. And, Witness, let me ask you some additional questions regarding this paragraph 11 of your statement where you talk about snipers who were in houses on the small hill next to Mount Hum called Stotina. That's what you're saying in your statement. Let me first ask you, how do you know there that were snipers in the area called Stotina?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I was born in the area, and this is where I played as a child. There were snipers in various locations, and I would respond to their fire, and I claim with full responsibility that I had to protect women and children and that I had to respond with fire to all the fire opened from various sniper nests. That's how I knew where those snipers were and how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me first ask you, from which army were these snipers?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: All the snipers that I personally saw walking about were from HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You're saying that you personally -- personally saw snipers working -- walking about. Can you give any specific units when you say they were from HVO units? Can you give names of specific unit?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I didn't know exactly what units they belonged to, but I was so close to them that I could see them. I knew them. I even knew their rifles. Through my binoculars I could even see the numbers on their rifle butts. If I saw them today, I would be able to recognise each and every one of those snipe shooters -- sharpshooters, because the distance between us was not more than 2 or 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. You've stated a couple of things. Let me first ask you: You've stated that you could see their rifles. Can you give the Court information as to what rifles these snipers were using?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could you -- just a moment. Wait. Could you describe -- you were at 200 metres and you could see them through your binoculars. Could you describe the appearance of those sharpshooters? How did they look?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were four of them as I was watching through the binoculars; one of them had grey hair. He had a pony-tail, and he had a hunting rifle with a sight, and he had black camouflage uniform. Another one was younger. He had a black bandanna on his forehead, and he wore the rifle that we call the bone breaker. The third one was in a striped blue and white T-shirt, and next to him was a young child with -- and there were some detainees with him. The last one who -- was at a bunker. He was thin and he wore a very special camouflage uniform. He wore a 12.7 sniper, the very large one. I was wondering why -- why there were two or three detainees around them. I didn't understand that behaviour. My colleague, who is now deceased, told -- showed me that that person was carrying his arm like this. And then when I looked I could see better that he was either wounded or his arm was crooked. I would still recognise him. He was very thin and his arm was bandaged, and his sniper was a very large one, the 12.7 sniper. This is what I saw on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just described the four individuals, and this is a good clarification because so far nobody has told us that there were prisoners around snipers. Who were the prisoners? Were they civilians? Were they members of the BiH army? The Serbs? Foreigners? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were civilians who had been brought from Heliodrom. One group was digging trenches and constructing bunkers and the other group, we couldn't see them well and he took them to the house, the three or four of them. I didn't allow my men to shoot. Only three or four hours later, when they came out of the house, we realised that these people had been digging holes in the wall as loopholes [as interpreted]. Only on the following day the snipers started opening fire. On that particular day, on the first day, fire was not opened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you well, you're saying that there were people who had been brought from Heliodrom with them. When one of these snipers opened fire, if they did, the civilians who were around them, the people who had been brought from Heliodrom, they witnessed the shots that came from Stotina; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is. That is precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, how do you know that the persons who were next to the snipers were prisoners; and secondly, how do you know that they had been brought from Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They wore civilian clothes, and they were sitting on the tops of the rocks on the separation line, so we could see them. We could see their faces. That's why we didn't shoot. They were so close to us that we could hear them talk amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At 200 metres we can indeed hear people talk. Did you actually hear the conversations? What were they saying to each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were afraid. I heard only a few of them saying, "If we only had water, to have a sip of water." On that day it was so hot that it was not easy to bear the heat without water. I did not dare give them any because I was afraid that I might be hit by one of the snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another thing that you indicated, but that was very fast; maybe that has escaped everybody else but it didn't escape me. You said that you had seen a young child next to one of the snipers. I'm wondering whether this was the sniper's child or whether this was a child that had been brought from somewhere, from Heliodrom perhaps, or maybe that was a child that resided in the neighbourhood. Who was the child?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The child appeared from the nearby house, and while the detainees were digging the trenches it was playing with a rifle. It was looking through the optical device. It was a 10-year-old boy who was playing with the rifle. I don't know whether the rifle was loaded. I suppose that it was, and that child was playing with the rifle, looking through the optical devise and things to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, in answer to -- to some of the questions of the Judges you gave a description of the four persons that you saw on that day, and you said two had camouflage uniforms. Were you close enough to see whether these camouflage uniforms also had badges on them and, if so, what kind of badges did they have?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I did not discern the insignia; they were small. But I know that they wore camouflage uniforms. The two of them, since it was hot, it was the month of July, they took their camouflage blouses off, and they walked in their T-shirts, and their uniforms were hanging on the door of that house all that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, how often were these snipers shooting in the area of Donja Mahala where you were operating?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: It depended on the situation. Sometimes two days would pass without a bullet being fired, and there were days when there was constant shooting from dawn to dusk. They had their reconnaissance and when they were advised that somebody was moving across the bridge they would start shooting. It was only when they had information that there were targets in sight they would open fire. They wouldn't do it randomly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, a question that I wanted to ask somebody for a long time but the witnesses that have been here so far probably could not have been able to answer. You are a perfect witness for this question, because you were the commander of 120 people in Donja Mahala. You've just told us that there were four snipers, that in July you saw four of them, and you added to that that from time to time they would open fire. They would shoot. Very well, then. There were four individuals. You were the commander of a group of 120 people who were not maybe there at the same time, but bearing in mind the potential danger of -- coming from these four persons, how come that your unity and you as their commander did not stage a command operation or any other kind of operation to take the control of that zone which was situated not more than a couple of hundred of metres away? You're saying that you could see them at a hundred to 200 metres' distance, and this is where their sniper nests were. How come that as the commander of that unit is didn't occur to you to take control of that zone? There were quite a few of us, and there were only four of them very close to you. Maybe behind them there were other elements that prevented you from doing that. I don't know. Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my company defended the zone from the Bulevar to Cekrk. I had 120 mean at my disposal on the line that was about three kilometres long. We did try to break through and we did take the situation on the area on the 21st of September. I found sniper -- snipers there. And then they had shelled us with howitzers. And if you -- if it ever happens that 10.000 of shells fall on you, then you understand. On the 22nd of September, they pulled Donja Mahala to the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 18 you say that on the 21st of September you tried a break-through and you found snipers. Did you -- did you imprison them? Did you arrest them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally led that group. Whatever was there before was either killed or arrested. Nobody was -- was either killed or fled. Nobody was arrested. I don't know how many were kill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was one who was killed? How many were killed on the HVO side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw three. On the Visnjica hill, I was wounded at that time, and I was dragging another wounded soldier. So I was wounded in the arm and in the leg. I barely pulled through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there was just a language subtlety there. I don't feel that the witness is answering the question you have asked him about. He's talking about a possible action at Stotina, but it's difficult to reconstruct it all because the sentences are not very well linked together, so there might have been some misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let me repeat the question, because I also realise that there was some problems of comprehension and interpretation. Let me ask the question again. I understood it that on the 21st of September there was an action on the part of the BH army, and you were in the Donja Mahala unit and its commander, that this action was against the lines held by the HVO. Now, I understood it that during this operation you told us that among the snipers that there were three who were killed. Of the snipers there were three who were killed and the other fled because you didn't arrest or take anyone into custody because everybody fled. Now, I understood it that during that operation you yourself were wounded. Is that the fact it have? Is that what you told us? If not, put us right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The action was a continuous one at Cekrk and Stotina and the upper part of Hum, and this action was led by my deputy so that I did not have an insight into the lower part of the action, because on that day 155 howitzers and 130 cannons attacked us so that there were shells falling on both sides of the positions, and there were both -- there were wounded on both sides and destroyed houses on both sides. So it was very difficult, a difficult situation, and it was all we could do to pull out and save our lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, what I'm interested in, Witness, is this: The action that concerns Stotina, within that action, the members of the HVO who were positioned at Stotina, were they wounded, killed, arrested, or did they flee? So that is my specific question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that. I don't have any information about that. I wasn't there on the spot. I was 150 metres away up on Hum. There were wounded on both sides, but as to the exact figures and information, I can't tell you more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So these three who were killed, where were they killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The three who were killed were killed 150 metres above Stotina at a hill called Visnjica. It's at a higher elevation. It's midway up Hum. So they had nothing to do with the action at Stotina and Cekrk. That was a separate group. We didn't expect it. We didn't know it existed. It was in the old Austrian bunkers, and they attacked this bridge with the 12.7 snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thanks to Mr. Kovacic, we have a much clearer idea of the events. So what you're saying is there was one action on the 21st of September, but before that at Stotina there was never any action of that order which would incapacitate the snipers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as a commander, I feel extreme pressure. When you experience people placing 1.000 civilians, unarmed civilians, men, women, and children, women carrying small children and they're shooting at them, well, we would have taken those positions very easily had there not been thousands of civilians. When the war broke out, Donja Mahala had 2.000 inhabitants. On the 1st ever August it had 5.000 inhabitants. They brought in so many civilians that they ate up all our food reserves, for example. And led me add this: Our water supply and electricity supply was cut off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, in your group of 120 men, did you not have your own sharpshooters, your own snipers to do what in military terms is called counter-sniping, particularly in reducing and eliminating the opposite side's positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't [as interpreted] have as many snipers as they had. We did have counter-sniping, but this was an action not led by 120 men but by 12. I led 12 men. The other men were deployed along the Bulevar to the old bridge to Semovac and along the Bulevar. So this action was actually only led by 12 men, and they were led by two commanders. One of them was killed. I was spared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for giving us those explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, but I'm told that there may have ban slight error in the translation. Could we ask -- could the question be posed again that you posed, Mr. President, whether they had as many snipers as the other side, because I think -- I'm told that the answer was that he indicated that they did have as many as the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Sir, I didn't ask you if you had as many snipers. I asked you whether in the group of 120 men, whether you had snipers, and your answer was that you just had 12 men to man the attack. Could you explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. A combat company who -- that -- the people who are commanders, generals, have a company of 126 men, and you know what a company has to have, two mortars and anti-armoured unit, two snipers, a sower, what we called a sower, and so on. Now, on our side people went into action when they were carrying the wounded, carrying food, and protected them when crossing open spaces. That's the only time they went into action. Ordinary people shot just to prevent a sniper from killing men, women, and children carrying water, because women and children would be killed when they went to fetch water around feels from kitchens and so on, and they were shot at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that in the company you had two snipers. Where were they positioned, those snipers? You said, "we had but two," only two, so where were they positioned, your two snipers? And two snipers within the company.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One was at Hum. We didn't have real sharpers. We didn't -- snipers. We didn't have the proper weapons. People didn't have the weapons people didn't have the weapons to defend themselves. We just had the ordinary M-48 rifles. They're Mauzer's of 7.9 calibre. They're not much to speak of had we had real snipers like the other side then nobody would have ever functioned from a sniper nest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect to the witness, I believe, now that he's hearing your questions, he's either confabulating or he's changing his testimony completely. He went from, "We had as many snipers as they did," then he indicated they had 12. Now he's down to two. Now he's not -- they're not even snipers. "We didn't have the weapons." I think the question should be posed, did they have as many snipers as the other side, because that's what the gentleman said on direct examination to your question, and now he's changing his testimony. And please remind him he's under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, in your language did you say that you had as many, just as many snipers as the HVO, or did you say that you had less, that you had two? What was it you said exactly? Could you be specific, because the Defence seems to be telling me, and Mr. Karnavas understands B/C/S, that you said that you had as many, just as many as the other side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge, I'm 57 years old. When the war began I was 42. This is what I said: We did not have adequate sniper weapons, but we did have anti-sniper activities against every sniper nest that was shooting at us. I was shooting, too, and I've taken the solemn declaration. There is no hole at Cekrk where I did not fire a hundred bullets. You don't know what it feels like when you see mothers and children, three, four, seven years old, are expelled by the shooting of a sniper and that's what happened to my mother and my daughter and my brother's family. They were expelled. Nobody can explain this to you unless you've experienced it. I was watching all this going on from Hum, and I couldn't do anything. It's not the same if your mother, who is 75 years old, is being shot at or your daughter-in-law, whoever. There was a 70-year-old woman who was shot at. And we targeted military persons. Had I had a tank, I would have shot them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is our concern to know whether your unit had what we have qualified in military terms as snipers. You said that you launched counter-sniper operations and that you yourself fired, and we understand that, you being a commander. But my question is a very precise one. In your particular unit in Donja Mahala, were there specialists who could shoot at the snipers of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's exact. We just had two men who were in charge of returning fire when they started targeting civilian targets and the people, when they killed someone, when they -- on the bridge. When they killed a woman and -- women and children. More men were hit and killed in carrying these wounded people here and there. So there were always dead and always people killed when we went to fetch those who had been killed and injured and carried them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said there were two. That's why I asked you the question a moment ago. I asked you whether those two men, those two men, whether they were positioned in general terms -- or where were they positioned in general terms? What was their position? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of them was positioned exactly in the direction of the Kamenica bridge near Hum, because that wasn't where the tyres fell. So he was only monitoring the situation at the bridge. The other was at Hum. The other was positioned at Hum, and I have to tell you that part of Hum descending towards Donja Mahala was under the BH army control. We had reconnaissance men there, intelligence men there, and other men who always monitored the situation in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of what you just said, can we conclude that in the positions facing Stotina, the four that you indicated, you did not position a sniper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't. I did not. I didn't have anybody to put there. Had I had someone, I would have put them there. Since I wasn't in the area myself all the time, I couldn't be there all the time, then that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is really not my intention to take away your time. I think that a lot of the problem arises from the following: The witness uses the plural "we" when he speaks about himself and when he speaks about his company of which he was the commander and when he refers to the whole of the BH army. That is my impression. He always uses the first person plural, the "we." I must say that I didn't understand half of what he said. I'm not clear on what he said at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, in your answers, would you please take care and distinguish what you yourself did in the area, that is to say you could say, "I," use the first person singular, and when you use the first person plural and say "we," you mean other people as well. Now, Mr. Bos, please proceed. We have ten minutes or a little bit before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, you've testified earlier that -- that you've seen several of these snipers yourself. I'm going to show you a photograph, and I'm going to ask you to make some comments on that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And if the witness could be shown -- if we can put this photograph on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this photograph? And if we could put the ELMO covering the whole --

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I do recognise this. This is the settlement behind Stotina which you could see from Hum only when you're up at Hum. You couldn't see it from Mahala. This one, that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If we can get a bit of a wider angle for this photograph, and if we can move maybe -- yeah. Can we get a wider angle of the complete photograph? Well, then we'll have to shift the photograph a bit. I wonder if it's not better to have another photograph. Let's use this one. Witness, can you -- can you indicate on this photograph where you saw snipers operating? And you can --

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: From left -- from right to left. The first sniper nest was in this small bit of wood here. The prisoners dug communicating trenches and trenches. The second sniper nest was here where there was a reconnaissance man, a scout. And the shooting came from that small window. And the third nest was here, and the fourth was over here. I can't recognise it, but anyway, they targeted Mahala directly, in a straight line. It was right by the Neretva, on the edge of the hill but you can't quite see it here on this photograph. And that's where the sniper with the 12.7 weapon shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, you've indicated four positions. Could I ask you with the marker to first mark -- you know, mark the first position with a circle and put a number 1 there. Could you put a number 1 at the first and -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And you're saying the fourth position isn't actually visible on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: It's over here, over here. Right that way, right that end, further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question about the -- the first position that you've indicated, because it seems that there's -- that this is -- that you indicated, you know, some bushes. What was actually there, because it's -- it's a bit difficult to see.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: There was a wall here, a two-metre wall with some weekend cottages over there. And the communicating trench was dug there and so he probably came there in the morning and waited there for the women and children came out to be able to -- we only saw this when the leaves fell, because they were deciduous leaves and we could see them once the trees were bare in this thicket here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, the houses that are depicted on this photograph, were all the houses there in 1993 as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes, but they've been built up now. They were destroyed, devastated by the Serb aggressor in 1992, because in 1992 there were Serb units here. But since then they've been refurbished.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated a fourth position which you are not able to mark on this map. Let me give you another photograph, Witness. Again, if we can put this on the -- maybe we can first get an IC number for the first photograph. Mr. Usher, if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Sir, on that first photograph you have put two numbers, 1, 2, 3, and 4. Could you place your initials there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just put three numbers, 1, 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 3. We can't see the fourth. Would you place your initials there, please. Put your initials there. Mr. Registrar, a number for the photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be given Exhibit number IC 417, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 417, IC 417, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, you've now been given another photograph. Again, do you recognise what this -- is depicted on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it very well. I went there three times in 1992 and 1993. I know the area very well. This is the entire area of Stotina - that's what it's called - and it's exactly 100 metres above sea level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, maybe -- again could you mark on this photograph with number 1, 2, 3 and 4 the four positions that you've been referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes, I can. One, two, three, and the fourth one was here. There was a bunker here, a bunker, a communicating trench which allowed entrance into this house, and the sniper was particularly active from that point number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You've marked four dots on the photograph. Could you give them number 1, 2, 3, 4, as you have indicated. Could you put a number 1, 2, 3, and a 4 next to these dots.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, on this photograph we can see the four points or positions where you saw the snipers. You yourself, where were you on this photograph when you saw them? Can you indicate to us the place you were at when you said you were able to see them?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: A little higher up Hum hill here in a cave called Crvena. And it says "We're all Tito's. We're all Tito." Because when Comrade Josip Broz Tito died, the people wrote up here, "We are all Tito," and you can see that place from the main road. And two men were there mostly. Not all the time, but mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, if I can make a follow-up question on this. Did the ABiH control the complete Hum mountain?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: No. No. The BH army couldn't. It just went on a need-to-go basis. We didn't dare appear there because we could have been hit by a shell. We didn't even have an ordinary gun, let alone a tank. And we didn't dare shoot from that spot to disclose our positions, our whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. If I understand you correctly, you said that you were in a cave that was called Tito's cave, and with your pen you indicated the direction, because apparently we can't see it on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, with a red pen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've indicated that you were above Stotina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in the direction -- it's about 250 metres above sea level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Two hundred and fifty metres. Now, you've put a dot on the white margin. So we have 1, 2, 3, 4, the four positions. Now, as the crow flies how far are those positions from your dot in the margin where you were, denoting the cave, the red cave where you were at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A maximum of 350 to 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So with your binoculars, you saw what you described to us; right? And the others, they -- or, rather, those four, they didn't know that you were very close to them? Didn't realise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they did not. They had absolutely no idea, because we didn't show ourselves at all. We didn't dare show ourselves, make any moves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The legal officer is asking for a larger map. Can you -- do you not, Mr. Bos, have a larger map so that we could see clearly where he was located?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe we can try this photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here. Exactly here at this spot. Do you want me to draw a circle there? Right here. There's a depression here, and we slept there. We spent the night there when it was cold. It sometimes rained. And we were there for two or three days and then went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe you could put a number 1 next to that circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And if we could get an IC number for this particular map, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can you now show the spots, the four spots, positions, where the men were that you were able to see, the numbers 1, 2, 3 and 4, the four positions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One, 2, 3, 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question from the Bench. On that map, Witness, can you also indicate the direction that the snipers were shooting at? What direction were they shooting with respect to the four points, 1, 2, 3, 4? Show us the direction, the trajectory of the shots when they were shooting, as you say, against civilians and the unarmed population.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That particular day or what, Your Honours? I don't understand the question. Do you mean on that day while I was watching or the whole month? Because we went there on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, to some extent the witness's last comment may confirm this. I just want this to be clear that the witness is being asked - again to avoid confusion - what he himself can say from his own personal observation so that we do have a clear distinction between what he can say and what he might be reporting second or third-hand or, worse, from somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I can show you what I saw hit in my neighbours' places, and I'm ashamed really. I saw them kill a cow here. They killed a horse there. On this side they killed a cow and a calf, a fowl. And in this little park they killed a cow and a mare, and they killed a horse over there. I issued an order, Your Honour, which was a curfew, to enforce a curfew from morning to night, and nobody was allowed to go out without our permission. And as soon as our scouts told us the sniper was up there we would hide the civilians. The only time when people could move around was at night. When their snipers had nothing to do, when they were idle, they first hit a dog at my house, and then they shooted at cats and anything else that was moving around in this area. All I can show you is where -- roughly where people were killed. I was -- I was at one place when three men were killed in the space of one day, and another man was wounded in the leg. The bone was broken, but he remained alive. I can't say anything else about the others who were killed because I wasn't there when they were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you had a scout, and this scout, where was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, below Pijesak. This was the safest place. No tyre from Hum could fall here, and this is where he -- was his reconnaissance command. The tyres would fall at the distance from -- of 300 metres to this -- houses was a natural hiding place against tyres. Usually those were young lads between 18 and 25 who were fast, who could run fast, who could go there and move around very quickly. I'm only sorry to say that a lot of them were killed. Actually, none of them stayed alive and they were all members of my unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The counsel has asked you a very important question. He wanted to know what you saw yourself and what you heard from others. Could you please be very precise and answer Mr. Stewart's question. At a given moment at any given place, did you yourself witness sniper shots that came from Stotina and that wounded, killed somebody or an animal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will just confirm that there were people who always remained alive, who survived. I was a witness in the month of August near this house. The man was Resezovic Kemal, and he worked with me. And Smaja Kljak was next to him. He was a well-known person in Mostar. He had a restaurant. He was an invalid. Both of them were killed -- wounded by a sniper, and the third person, Zulfo Maric, is still alive but was wounded. This is what I saw with my own two eyes. I was 50 metres away from the place. This is my house here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what was the exact date when you witnessed that? Do you remember the date when this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember the date. I know it was in the month of August. I'm sure that it was August, but I can't remember the date, because at the time I was also wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, it was in the month of August, and -- and the shots, where did they come from? You were there. You saw everything at a distance of 50 metres. Where did the shots come from on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, from this house here, in this direction. It was a straight line from this house to the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it should be said that the translation has not been recorded correctly because the witness speaks too fast, and I believe that there is a problem with the witness's testimony. I would like to point out to page 39, line 7. I believe that the witness said that Mr. Resezovic Kemal, who was together with him, was carrying something. And you mentioned the name of that thing, and we may conclude that it was a weapon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a pot for lunch.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. And I believe that next to him there was a person who was walking who was bedridden.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, he had suffered a stroke. It was Kljak Smaja. The whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina knows that man. Everybody knows him. You know him. I'm sorry that now he's dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to make a 20-minute break and we will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we continue maybe we still need two IC numbers for two of the maps that have been marked, and so if I could ask the witness to put his signature on this map and also the map underneath it, and if we can get two IC numbers for these maps. Maybe --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If we can show the map which is now on -- on the ELMO, and if we can get an IC number for this particular map. This is the second map that was shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The smaller map will be given Exhibit number IC 418, and the larger map of Stotina will be given Exhibit number IC 419.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Both of them are large maps. The smaller map has already been given a number which is IC 417. So could this be IC 418?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. They will be 418 and 419.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to move on to another topic, but I have just one more question. You've spoken about an ABiH attack on the 21st of September. What I wanted to know is, did the ABiH take over the area of Stotina on -- on the 21st of September? Did they take control over that area after that attack?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I now ask you, Witness, to look at Exhibit 01017 in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I have an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What is you want to say, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: You have forgotten two snipers on the top of Hum which were lethal and which managed to kill everybody they shot at. Nobody survived their action, and you've forgotten those two sniper nests on Hum.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have just told us that we have forgotten two snipers on the top of Hum which also opened fire, which were deadly. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And these snipers, what happened to them? Were they killed? What happened to these snipers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't even see those snipers. I only know that every bullet they fired killed a man because it was shot at a diagonal of 90 degrees, and they would shoot a man in the neck. The exit wound would be around the kidney area because it came from the hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying that -- that you saw these snipers or you were told about them? Are you just speculating, or did you actually see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw them through the binoculars, and they wounded me as well. I looked at them shooting, and I can point their exact places to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the interpretation it says that you were wounded by one of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When was that? When were you shot at? On what day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 23rd and 24th September, 1993. In between these two days when the operation was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I observe, this is getting, with respect, completely out of hand. Ms. Alaburic is doing the cross-examination of this witness, but Your Honours will appreciate I'm on my feet because sniping has come up and we're in this case together anyway. What the witness has been doing has been mentioning in very sweeping, general terms matters which in many instances are not even alluded to in his statement, but we should, with respect, remind ourselves that when we were dealing over the last two or three weeks with the sort of incident which the witness has just mentioned in a sentence or so, we spent perhaps two, three hours considering just that incident and just the details of that incident in a detailed, proper way with then a proper opportunity to cross-examine, and those detailed incidents formed the basis of the expert report, or they're the foundation, and the expert report looked at those in detail. What we're getting from this witness are a series of assertions which are like the one-line summary in the report which was no more than really alerting everybody to what it was we're going to have to deal with by thorough evidence. This is a completely inappropriate and unfair way of dealing with these subjects. It simply does not present the case properly and does not give the Defence remotely a fair opportunity to grapple with these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If I could just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, don't confuse the matter. The expert testimony is one thing. The statement of a witness is another thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With respect, I wasn't. I wasn't confusing and I want to make that clear. I mentioned the expert report, but I was concentrating particularly on the way in which that series of factual witnesses fed into the expert report. Those things went together, and it was apparently because it was acknowledged that the incidents had to be examined one by one in detail that the factual witnesses came -- came here, Your Honour. So, please, I'm not -- even if I may appear to be, I wish to make it clear I'm not confusing those issues. The contrast is primarily between the sort of factual evidence sought to be given today and the sort of factual evidence given in relation to those incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If I could just briefly respond to this in this particular evidence with respect to snipers on Hum hill is something the witness is referring to in paragraph 11 of his statement, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In about three words, 10 words. That's my point, Your Honour. You can't just say something like that and then go into all these details. I've made my point about the contrast with the other witnesses anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, let's focus our attention on Exhibit 01017, which I think you have in front of you. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I do. I'm familiar with this document. This is a document issued by the local commune of Donja Mahala, which was the closest to the place where shells were falling as well as tyres from Hum hill. And they kept the record on the dead, wounded, burnt houses, and everything that happened during the night. Such things always happened after 10.00 in the evening. I can slow down a little if you want me to. This was written by a man who buried all people in the courtyard of the house because -- actually, it was a school, because we didn't have the time to bury them in a cemetery. We buried them next to each other in gardens, in courtyards, in the school courtyard. So much from me on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what was the name of the man who -- who has written this report? Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: He's still alive. Nedzad Basic is his name. He was the commissioner of the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have a problem because we don't have the Croatian original of the document. We only have the English translation and the witness is obviously commenting upon the English version, or he's looking at something else that we don't have. We only have the English translation. And we only got a small portion of that if we look at what the witness has before him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If I can clarify, Your Honours. This was a document which was in both B/C/S and English. The original document was in both languages so that why there isn't a translation. The document has six pages and it has three of B/C/S language and three in English, in English language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid there must be some confusion then, because I have a document in my hand, P 01017, and it is less than half page English. There is no Croatian original, and we check and we didn't get it, and it seems that the other Defences as well didn't get it. But maybe I'm wrong. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, the complete document has an ERN range from 1813 to 1819 so the complete document has in fact seven pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It's interesting that all the Defences are having just this one-page document and which is less -- it is about one-third of the page on English. Nobody seems to have anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you will allow me an explanation for my learned friend from the Prosecution. In the chart that was submitted to us as regards this document for this witness, it says that this document has only one page because the last number -- digits are 1819 to 1819 [as interpreted]. Without any doubt this is only one page. Maybe we could place the document on e-court and this would allow us to see the B/C/S version that we don't have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please put the B/C/S version on the e-court. Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we really try to prepare ourselves professionally in order to answer all the questions when we receive material, but how can one do that if we don't know the date when something happened, when a death occurred, if we don't know whether the person in question was a woman, a man, a soldier, where the incident occurred, how it occurred, from which position it was shot or is it thought that shots came from? We cannot examine this witness based on documents we received, at least in this part, because we don't know when, how, where, date, medical documentation, nothing. We don't have any of those things that would assist the Defence and us accused to prepare ourselves and to put such questions that would lead to the resolution of this situation. We only get our stories and then facts are incorporated in those stories to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, this document which was drafted by the municipality of Donja Mahala, in B/C/S and in English, this document, was it disclosed to the Defence according to Article 68 and 66 of the Rules of Evidence and Procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document is certainly in e-court, and I don't know if I can draw a conclusion from that that if it's in e-court that it should also have been disclosed to the Defence. I mean, as far as I can say that, yes, the complete document was disclosed, but I base that on the fact that it is in e-court. But, Your Honours, I just have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: -- one question on this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Mr. Ibrisimovic has asked the floor. He wants to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
