utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Obviously the course of this examination shows that Mr. Karnavas was absolutely right. What I'm trying to say is another thing. The statement from this witness was taken in 2005. Whatever the Prosecutor is asking now he could have asked during the interview of this witness. I'm going to quote you: When the procedure was established according to 92 ter Article, you said that the Prosecution cannot disclose a statement and then introduce new elements to the statement. This is a typical examination of such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received the number of documents in the proofing and irrespective of the fact whether we have it or not we download it from various systems. However, the document that is now on the screen corresponds in number. The number is ERN -- this ERN number does not correspond. But this is a different document. It has a different ERN number. It has nothing to do with what we were given as P 01O017 [as interpreted]. Irrespective of the time when it was disclosed to us, it is simply a different document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, the Defence says that this document P 01017 that they have does not correspond with what they see on the screen. There is a mismatch between the number and the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We have just pulled up the records, and according to our records, this document was disclosed to the Defence on the 12th of November 2005 as an attachment to the statement of this witness. This document was actually attached to the statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, One page. One page, one page was, you know, now you're showing four pages. It was one page. Now just confess error and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- our record says that there were six pages disclosed. The ERN range is 13 to 19. It's -- but, Your Honours, I can move on because I only have a question in relation -- well -- MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise to my learned friend. I would just like to say by way of explanation there is difference between the P number and the ERN number. The ERN number is in the right-hand corner. It is typed out. And when the P number is disclosed then the document is searched for by the ERN number. The ERN we received with the document or the document that we have downloaded, one can see that this is the ERN number that was given to us in the chart and that we have down loaded the right document. The document that the Prosecution informed us about. The ERN number on the screen is different from the ERN number on the chart. In order to avoid any confusion, if we put this document on the ELMO, you will see that the ERN numbers do not correspond to each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Usher, could you please go and fetch the document from Mrs. Tomic and could you please put it on the ELMO. They will then this be able to compare the two ERN numbers. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance. Now that you look at it, here, in the upper right corner, you can see 04231819. Go back to the front page, please. Put the front page back. This is the number. Now turn to the proofing chart for this witness. The number -- the next page, please. The number here corresponds to the number of the document. It is encircled 04231819, and this is the ERN number, and I believe that the situation is clear now. I believe that now you understand what we have been trying to communicate to you all this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I now understand what -- what the problem is, and thank you, Counsel, for clarifying, because I didn't realise what the problem was. What's been explained here is that this -- what we see now on the screen is the exhibit list that was -- that was submitted to the Defence for this particular witness, and it seems here there's -- there's a mistake in the ERN number because it only says 19, 19, and it should have said 1813 up to 1819. So it was disclosed, but if you work on the basis of this list you would think only this one page would have been disclosed -- would have been used. So I understand the difficulty, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Before -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The learned friend is right. Just one page was given to us and this is precisely what we are saying. Irrespective what it says in the database, we received just one page. This is correct. We don't know whether this document maybe has 17 pages. Nobody knows. Just the Prosecutor knows. Nobody else does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: If I understood it correctly, Mr. Bos said that that was what they have disclosed was not only one page but with a wrong number. But let us listen to him to clarify if -- what was really the problem. But before he will be doing that, let me also say that the Chamber has displayed flexibility this morning when we ruled that actually the cross-examination will be continued on Monday, and really I would like to ask all of us here around the table and in the courtroom to -- to be flexible enough also and to continue our audience here. As a matter of fact, the -- as you recall, the Prosecution received one and a half hours to present its case and the Defence two and a half hours, which means one hour more, and therefore I believe that the Defence will have the opportunity to be prepared during the -- the rest of the week and during the weekend. I know that it is a bit of rather urgent issue which could have been avoided otherwise, but I also would like to recall that we are here a quarter past 11.00, and the Prosecution was not given the chance to finish its -- its direct. So I would like to ask everyone now to proceed in a calm manner and to finish with this issue in due time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If we could just look at the page which the Defence also has, that one page that was shown on the e-court. Witness, you have this document in front of you. Now, we spoke about the document briefly. Now, reading this paragraph, and if you read the six -- the sixth line from the bottom, does it read that: "On the 9th of November, 1993, Ustashas from HV and HVO bombed the old bridge"? Can you read that sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel. Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's working now. Your Honours, I apologise. I'm really embarrassed to interrupt, but at the beginning of the whole thing we said that this short document is not the one that we have. That line does not exist in our text. We have something else. The Prosecution doesn't want to understand this. Give us a five-minute break. Let us compare our papers. Let us see what we've got. It seems that we are talking at cross-purposes. It is as if we were speaking German and the Prosecution was speaking Dutch. Again, he has given us a document that we do not have at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, you have put a question on the document that finishes with numbers 1816, and they're saying they have 1819, and that in the document with finishing in digits 1819, nothing is mentioned to the effect describing the old bridge. This is what Counsel Kovacic has just repeated. I don't want to lecture you, Mr. Bos, but first of all there is a mistake in the provision of your services. You have disclosed to Defence a document under number 1819, and the Prosecution is now drawing your attention -- attention to the fact that they have the document in English 1816, 1817, and 1818. I will not -- going to insist. If I were you I would just move on to something else. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for being a nuisance, but my colleague has just checked the e-court and we have established that the integral document that the Prosecution is trying to convince us that it was disclosed was placed on e-court earlier today. So we couldn't see it. We didn't have an opportunity to see it. Since we have lost so much time, we believe that this document is nothing but a political pamphlet which has nothing to do with the truth, and I'm sure that even if it is admitted it will not be taken into consideration. This is nothing but a political pamphlet, but we will hear from witness. We have now wasted a lot of time because some things have not been disclosed properly. This is a media report. If we have -- if it boils down to us dealing with letters written by a local commune to the UNPROFOR and other bodies as a report for the media, I truly believe that we are wasting our very precious time here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, can I ask you, where were you around the 8th and the 9th of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I was on the 8th of November, 1993, in Donja Mahala at my mother's and at my mother's in law, because on the 9th of November my father-in-law and my mother-in-law were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And could you tell us what happened on that day, and the 8th of November?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: The 8th of November I came by to have a cup of coffee and I heard a tank firing a -- two or three shots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, there must be a mistake. In the English translation it says that you were in Donja Mahala on the 8th of November visiting your mother, because on the 9th of November you mother and father-in-law were wounded. There as something wrong here. You could not have anticipated what -- what would happen 24 hours later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. No. No. This is a misunderstanding. This is a misunderstanding. On the 11th of August, on the 11th of August my father-in-law, Huso Bajgoric, was killed, and on the 8th of November the old bridge was shelled. I apologise. You can check with -- in the papers. My father-in-law was killed on the 11th of August at 5.00 in the afternoon, and on the 8th of November the old bridge was shelled. I apologise. Check the document and you will see that I'm telling truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, you have just stated that on the 8th of November the old bridge was shelled. Can you give us a bit more detail about what you saw that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: After the third shell fell - I will talk slowly, and I apologise - I went to the observation point called Izgorenistan [phoen]. This is the address Gojka Vukovica 118. The burnt flat was the ownership of Abdul Harakmani [phoen]. He is dead now. His flat burned down. He had three observation points in his apartment: One facing the Neretva, the other facing Stotina and Hum, the third facing the position from which the tyres were falling. Since I had shelter behind a fence I had binoculars and because of the snipers I didn't dare look. If I had looked, I would not have been sitting here. The artillery men know that every shell is seen. When a tank is firing from a distance of 2.000 metres you can see every shell and I was counting them, ladies and gentlemen of the jury, Judges, your Honourable Judges. I spent some three or four hours there. The shell was firing for two or three hours. The tank was shelling for two or three hours. Sometimes a shell at a time, sometimes two or three shells at a time. All that time I was on the balcony. The women and children came and we were observing some 40 or 50 shells falling all around Mostar. And this lasted for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in the document that the Prosecutor has shown you coming from the local commune, the date there is the 9th of November, 1993. That's the date mentioned there for the shelling of the bridge. Now, you're referring to it as happening on the 8th of November; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, gentlemen, the old bridge was destroyed on the 8th of November, and it fell on the 9th of November at 1015 hours, but it was destroyed on the 8th of November. It was shot four times on four occasions throughout the day. The fourth shelling, when I was in Radobolja it was hit by 60 or 70 shells in that day. So in the evening when we arrived you couldn't cross the bridge. I tried but had to go back. And it's absolutely astounding that it survived throughout the night. But the next morning I was at the Ruza hotel, and the gentlemen are fully aware of that, and around 10.00 a.m. -- I didn't have a watch, but about 10.00 a.m. we didn't have any water. The tank shot at us again, shot a fifth shell, and with the sixth shell the bridge fell. We were at hotel Ruza 150 metres away from the old bridge. There was a large cloud of smoke and the bridge fell. And the men started celebrating when they saw this. I went outside to calm the people down, and I believe that they were celebrating when it finally fell. And 15 minutes later my best colleague was killed by a sniper shot. So that -- that is the truth of it. It is as true as I am sitting here before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, you just stated that -- that in answer to the question of the Judge that on the 8th of November the bridge was shelled four times. Can you tell us exactly when those times were and what happened on each of these times?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: It was targeted in intervals -- at two-hour intervals at 8.00, at 10.00 and little afternoon and sometime between 3.00 and 4.00 in the afternoon. The shells damaged it so much that quite simply -- you know when a shell hit the old bridge you would have the mushroom effect. I saw it, and it's interesting to see, but it's a very sad sight. It is a black and yellow cloud of smoke in the form of a mushroom. And we were in Radobolja. And shrapnel from the shells fill on us so we had to flee, get out of the area and get away from the old bridge. Some 200 metres away from the old bridge this was. So the old bridge was destroyed on the 8th of November. It was totally destroyed, but it fell on the 9th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a question. You were talking about a tank fired. Did you see the tank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't. All the I saw was the barrel, the barrel shooting, and it changed positions. And whoever looked was probably targeted. We didn't dare raise our heads at all for fear of being targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know at which location this -- you said you saw a barrel. At what location did you see that barrel?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I apologise. The location was at Cekrk hill, Hum.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Later on I'll show you a photograph where you -- maybe you can mark that location, but let me just ask you a few more questions. You spoke about four intervals. Could you just tell us for each interval how many times -- how many shells would fall on each of these intervals?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really do apologise. I don't know the exact amount of ammunition that a tank has, combat sets a tank has. I'm not a tankist, but I know in one minute it is able to fire three to four shells. So when you have a burst of gunfire this would make it 20 or 30 shells. I might be wrong, but I don't know how you actually fire from a tank and how many the crew manning the tank actually fired. I don't know the terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How many shells in total were fired in the direction of the bridge that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure, but I do know there were between 60 and 70, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You've stated that in the evening of the 8th of November you actually went to the bridge. Can you explain again why you went to the bridge and what you did there?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: In the evening when it became dark people asked to go and see. I wasn't alone. There was -- there were 15 to 20 of us. I stood at the top of the bridge, and it was all -- well, you couldn't cross. I tried to get across, but I had to go back. And it's really amazing how it managed to stay up that long.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you describe the condition of the bridge when you were up there?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: When you get up onto the bridge, on the right-hand side was completely destroyed. There was a big hole. The railing fell. There was some sort of protection. There were three or -- three holes of a half-metre diameter. I don't know how I didn't fall through the bridge when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You've stated that that evening you stayed at the Ruza hotel. How far is the Ruza hotel from the old bridge?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: A maximum of 150 to 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And then you've also stated -- well, let me just ask you. What happened on -- you've spoke about it a bit, but let me ask you again. What happened on the 9th of November?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: On the 9th of November we went out onto the plateau facing the old town at the Ruza hotel. It was 10.00, 10.15. I didn't look at my watch. We didn't have anything to drink, so we went to have a drink. There was a small stream there, Radobolja. So we went to wash our faces and have a drink. So when the first shot, 10.00, 1010 hours, we didn't have any watches so we weren't able to tell the time, but it was a nice, fine, sunny day, and there were four shells that followed. I counted them exactly. The sixth one the sixth one hit the old bridge and it toppled into the water. On the 11th [as interpreted] of November six shells hit the bridge. I didn't see where the tank was firing from. I didn't dare put my head up because there was a sniper up at Hum. So it was only in the evening at around 10.00 p.m. that we went to have a look and there were just seven steps left standing and the bridge had toppled. And I can add that the people who had -- didn't experience this, there was general panic. Men, women, children, the elderly, the refugees, displaced persons who had come to Mahala. Took us two days to calm the situation down. And God forbid that anything like that happens again. And it's a real miracle that I survived. I don't know how. Although I didn't want to survive because I lost everything I held dear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, just before you continue I think we need to make a clarification in the record. On page 58, line number 14, you've stated that on the 11th of November six shells hit the bridge. Was it the 11th of November?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: The 9th of November. The 9th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If we can maybe now show the witness Exhibit IC 419, which was one of the photographs that was -- that he already marked. It's the last big photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, this is an aerial photograph -- well, again, do you recognise what's -- well, you recognised the photograph. You've already made some markings.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Bridge, Cekrk, the colony, the Hasan Brkic bridge, the Kamenica bridge. You can't see the old bridge on this photograph. Ah, I apologise. Well, you can't see it very well. Here it is over here. You can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, maybe just to clarify because this is an aerial photograph of several years ago when I think the old bridge was -- was not in the state as it is now. Could you maybe mark with a number -- we'll use numbers -- letters now. Could you mark a letter A where the old bridge is located on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this was a bridge which was white, built by the Spanish Battalion. It was a makeshift bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And could you now please mark a number B where you saw the barrel of the tank.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And if the usher maybe could just -- so we can saw see.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Roughly. Over here. Next to this house here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And, Witness, could you mark a number C where you were on the 8th of November.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: The first time -- you mean the 8th or the 9th?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The 8th of November, when you witnessed this shelling.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: The first two shellings I was in Mostar at the Zridaci [phoen], and second I was in Barakovina [phoen] near the river, and I saw the old bridge falling when I was at the Ruza hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You -- you've -- but you've marked a dot over there. Could you maybe put a number C where you've placed a dot on the map. Your Honour -- Witness, let me just ask you this: Could you mark letter number C where you actually saw the barrel of the tank. From where were you when you saw the barrel of the tank. Could you there put the number -- the letter C. No. That's where the barrel was, but where you saw the barrel, your position.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: In the burnt down flat in Gojka Vukovica Street 118.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, did the shelling stop after the 9th of November when the bridge had collapsed?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: No. The shelling did not stop. The -- the shelling of the Kamenica bridge started straight away from another position, in fact. And that's when the Kamenica bridge was destroyed. And there was a terrible panic among the population because Donja Mahala was completely cut off. We couldn't cross at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Only at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you mark on this map the location of -- of the Kamenica bridge with a number D.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And when did this -- was this bridge destroyed? On what date?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: It was destroyed on the 10th of November, sometime in the afternoon. One day after the old bridge. I know that it was sometime in the afternoon. About 1700 hours, maybe. The upper part was destroyed completely. I don't know how to mark that, but this area here, and it fell to the -- into the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I would now like to ask you to look at document -- I think we're done with the map. Could I ask you to look at Exhibit 04265.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have an IC number? Do you need one?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We already have an IC number for this photograph. We had marked it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, Your Honour. I apologise, but I didn't show you the location of the tank that fired on the 10th of November. And my colleague targeted the tank with a hand grenade, but he -- or, rather, a mortar, but he missed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the photo again, please so that he can show us the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, maybe you can mark that with the letter E, the position of the tank that hit the Kamenica bridge.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: We targeted it here from a hand -- by a hand-held rocket launcher. And the main scout was killed. I'm sorry about that. We targeted it with a hand-held rocket launcher. Let me say that my colleague who filmed all this died on the 30th, I think, before the new year, and the tape was handed over to someone. The cassette was handed over to someone, but it was lost subsequently. And may I just added that a Scot -- an Irishman from UNPROFOR filmed it all but left in an unknown direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, can I now ask you to look at Exhibit 4265 in your bundle. Is it correct, Witness, that I showed you this document yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I saw this document for the first time yesterday. I didn't know about it before, so thank you, gentlemen, for showing it, and it shows that Napalm bombs were thrown on --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to comment on what was said in the document it talks about an incident at 10.00 in the evening of the 16th of August, 1993 where it says a Napalm bombing trial operation was conducted. Do you remember what happened on the 16th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: On the 16th of August. You made a mistake. The 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You're absolutely right the 16th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that we have a problem with the interpretation or the translation. The witness said in line -- in 15, page 62, he said that this was the first time --"Yesterday I saw it for the first time." That doesn't -- he's saying that he sees for the first time that these Napalm bombs were falling. So he didn't know about it. He didn't see it in the real life, and you can't see that from the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, that's not how I understood it. I understood it that he saw the document yesterday, and he added that he confirms the Napalm bombings. But let me ask the witness a question to avoid all misunderstanding and ambiguity. Sir, yesterday you were shown this document; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, when you saw this document, what conclusion did you draw from it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That that night I was carrying three of my dead neighbours. I'll answer you, sir. I'll answer your question, sir. On the 16th of August, at around 2200 hours I was at Cekrk. I heard a plane flying overhead, and I shot it using my automatic rifle. It was a Kalashnikov. I shot 30 bullets. The first bomb fell -- fell just 10 to 15 metres away from my own house. It killed Kalalid Samira [phoen]. My other brother, he was killed on the 11th of August, the first one. The other bomb fell in Donja Mahala just before the Kamenica bridge. Envir Ornjica [phoen] was killed just by the mosque and Mustafa Pilagic [phoen]. And the only person that was still living but was wounded was Mr. Hakija Klaric [phoen]. I don't know how he remained living. I apologise to the gentleman. I'm not a linguist; I'm not a poet. I'm not Jasinj [phoen]. I'm a machine operator and I worked for 20 years with machines, machinery, and I know exactly what fell on me. Had an American Napalm bomb fallen on me, everything would have been burnt. It was a Djua [phoen] bomb, because I worked in the aeroplane factory, the Pesane [phoen] French company, and it is the best Duran [phoen] that is produced for the wings of an aeroplane. So with all due respect to the Defence counsel, you don't have to teach me anything where technology is concerned. You might put me right linguistically but I know everything there is to know about the machines and technology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you still haven't answered the question. Yesterday the Prosecutor showed you this document. Now, this document is being shown to you again today. What do you have to say to the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bombs fell, but there was no fire. Nothing was aflame. You just could smell this unpleasant smell. We didn't know what had happened. And I just said that on that day bombs did fall but I don't know what kind of bombs and I still don't know what the fill of the bombs was. All I know is that there was a detonation. I know what a Napalm is. If there was a Napalm bomb, then one kilometre -- US-produced, American Napalm bomb, then the whole area would have gone up in flames. I don't think we really have proper Napalm bombs because I worked for 20 years in the aviation industry, in the Sokol company from 1981 to 1992. I know each individual part of an aeroplane. If I might be allowed to explain. I worked for the Douglas aircraft, the Mirage, Boeing, Aleutian [phoen], all different kinds of aircraft. So I know all about this. You can't teach me anything about the aviation industry or air bombs. I know all about them. That's what I want to tell you. You can check out my knowledge, how much I know, and then you'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is the following: This document, the document we have here coming from the HVO indicates that on the 16th of August at 2200 hours there was a bombing operation, a Napalm bombing operation that was conducted. Now, this document, does it correspond to what you yourself observed on the ground, with what you experienced on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really do apologise, Your Honour, but three bombs fell, and three bombs exploded, and you could smell -- there was a very bad check out my knowledge, how much I know, and then you'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is the following: This document, the document we have here coming from the HVO indicates that on the 16th of August at 2200 hours there was a bombing operation, a Napalm bombing operation that was conducted. Now, this document, does it correspond to what you yourself observed on the ground, with what you experienced on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really do apologise, Your Honour, but three bombs fell, and three bombs exploded, and you could smell -- there was a very bad smell which affected your nose and throat. And three bombs fell along the street in Mahala. So all I can say is that the bombs did explode. Now, in those bombs, what substance was in those bombs I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: One follow-up question on this. The fact that there was this smell was that usual for bombs that they had this particular shell -- this smell or was this particular bomb smelling different than -- than usual?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Excuse me. I apologise, but "than usual." That means that there was a bombing campaign going on. So he indicated that there were three -- that there were three bombs allegedly. So the usual part denotes a fact that is not in evidence. I would appreciate it if counsel did not take liberties with the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Is this the only time that bombs fell on Donja Mahala?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was the begin the bombing. It was only the second time. I can't claim -- it wasn't the end of the bombing of Mahala. It was the beginning of the bombing. Perhaps the second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you say the second time. On how many times did -- did bombs fell on Donja Mahala? Bombs being dropped from an aeroplane.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: On the 17th of September, about 23, 24 hours. I remember that night very well because there were bombs dropping from planes and tyres being rolled down Hum. Some exploded while they were still on Hum, but I was in the local commune, at a place called Spile near Dugaric's bakery. One bomb fell on to Mehic Gara's [phoen] house. He was at Heliodrom at the time. And, gentlemen, it destroyed three houses completely and seven round about. His father's house and his brother's houses were shattered, and I can claim with my own life that Suada's -- I found Suada's head in the next door yard. It's very difficult for me to speak of those things. I couldn't ever have conceived of such a strong explosion. And the Donja Mahala road towards Cekrk was full of the debris of a house that had been blown up right across the road. So you couldn't walk down that road. You had to clear the debris and the rubble first. So that's what I wanted to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And you've been talking now about the 17th of December [sic], and on that occasion did -- was there the same -- was there the same --

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: The 17th. The 17th of September. I apologise. It was the 17th of the 9th month, September.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: That's -- that's what I said as well. And was there the same type of smell when the bombs fell on the 17th of September?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I can't confirm that exactly. It was all terrible. There are quite a lot of living survivors in the local commune who will be better placed to explain it all. I wasn't on the spot. I was 500 metres away from that spot, so that as the Donja Mahala area comes under strong winds, all the dust went towards Cekrk. So actually I couldn't feel anything. I just saw the houses that had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, okay, let's move on to one other exhibit which is Exhibit 9517. And I would like that, which is the Mostar map, which I would like the registry to have it shown on e-court, please. Witness, in paragraphs 13, 14, and 15 of your written statement you talk about the HVO practice of rolling tyres with explosives from Mount Hum into Donja Mahala. Now, I'm not going to ask you any questions about it because it's all in your statement, but the only thing what I would like you to do is -- and the map is going to be shown to you on the screen, is whether you could indicate which part of Donja Mahala was actually targeted with these tyres, where you mark that with a -- with a pencil on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And maybe the usher can assist so he can do this electronically.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, no. Don't use that marker, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes. So please indicate exactly the area where these tyres would hit Donja Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: The tyres fell at some 300 metres from the bridge. The first one fell here next to Sejo Besic's house. If you measure that, this is 350 steps or 300 metres. They could not fall here. That's why our command was here, because there is a canyon through which the tyre cannot pass. This is where it fell and this was the biggest tyre. If you walk through Donja Mahala now and if you count the craters, the red roses, as we call them, you will find 13 of them. For some people this number is lucky. For some unlucky. There were iron sheets so we barricaded all the passages so the tyres could not pass through. Two of them broke. One hit the house of Dr. Djino Kajtaz, a very well known doctor, pulmonologist. It hit one of his windows and then ricocheted but then we found that tyre. Your Honours, gentlemen, this was not a tyre. That tyre contained five or six tank shells. There were 20 or 30 kilos of explosive. There were wires attached to that tyre, and all that was ignited, and we could observe the tyre being pushed from the top, burning. And what it says here 1.15, 1.14, 1.18, this is the time when the tyre hit Mahala and how much time you have to find shelter in the garden. If I tell you that one of them broke some 150 metres away from me and I hurt all over, from my head to my genitals, that I could barely walk for three days. The doctor told me that I was lucky that my mouth was zipe [phoen] and otherwise my lungs would have burst. This is as much as I have to say in response to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About the tyres. You said the tyres contain the tank shells, 20 to 30 kilos of explosive, and also the ignition devices. And you said you observed it rolling down and then exploding because it had a ignition device. Where the person who rolled it down at the moment, where did that person -- how did that person ignite the explosive? How did it function? How did it work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was not shell -- shell -- tank shell but anti-tank mines, green mines that we call "hat mines." And the tyre was rolling there was an igniting device in there and on the side there were four or five devices, and as the tyre was rolling these ignition devices would ignite on the spot. When they pushed it and they ignited it up there, it took the tyre three and a half points get to the Donja Mahala and then it would explode. And you could hear the tyre rolling down the hill. There are lots of living witnesses. A lot of them were wounded. And I'm really amazed how come you called me, because there are other people who had been wounded and they could tell you much more than I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the story of the tyres is something that concerns me a lot, and the Chamber. You were a soldier. You know that during combat the armies have to act according to international rules of war, and the commanders have to do that. And if the army is not under control it's very difficult to control military target, but you say you were about 150 metres away from the place where the tyre hit, where -- the place of impact. You yourself, your company, were you situated in the vicinity of the place where this tyre landed? In other words, that tyre, according to you, was it targeted at you and your company or was it sent down randomly to target civilian population or nobody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This area is inhabited. There are white buildings that have in the meantime been rebuilt and floors have been added to them. There were no troops here. All the civilians were in the military -- in the elementary school and all the civilians slept in the basement. So nobody dared spend a night in this area. There was nobody who dared spend a night. All the population fled the area, and this zone was simply empty. There was nobody there. They only returned around the new year of 1994 when all the shelling had stopped. There were no military targets there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I'm trying to understand. You're saying that the zone had been deserted. How come that there were victims if there was nobody there? How come there were casualty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the first of them fell, people did not know what had hit them. The second one, when that one exploded, it appears the basement wall, 40 centimetres thick, made of concrete, at Gojka Vukovica 50. That's the address. Aida Delic was there and some other women were there and were wounded. Some other people were wounded. But it was the local commune that was recording that and not the army. Then all the population was evacuated to the basement of the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take the second tyre that is about to explode and it's -- be -- appears the 40 centimetre thick wall. You have given us the address. Gojka Vukovica number 20 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was 50. Number 50, number 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay it's a good thing I asked the question because the number was wrong. Okay. At that address were there any BiH members present? Were there any troops there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I came with full responsibility that that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to show you one more document, which is Exhibit 9328. And if you could get your bundle again. 9328. It's a document. It's not a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe the usher can assist to get the document. Okay. Well, we have it now, I think. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What can you say about this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: It is a request by the local population of Donja Mahala who had accommodated a lot of refugees, and they wrote an appeal, a letter to UNPROFOR. At that moment we were not aware of that letter at all, so -- but since we're in the position that we were in, the UNPROFOR received this letter, and as far as I can remember, towards the end of August a Spanish Battalion delegation visited Donja Mahala. And this is all I can tell you about this document. They brought food, water, and some medical supplies and toiletries for the women and children, and is all. That's the long and the short of it about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, the document doesn't have a date, but can you estimate approximately when this document was written down?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: In my view it was in the month of August. I don't know exactly because this was drafted by the local commune and I don't think I was there. But approximately it was in the month of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour the gentleman indicated initially he had no knowledge of the document. Now he's being asked when the document was drafted and sent over. Now he's speculating. This is clearly improper direct examination. Anywhere else in the world would nobody would ask this gentleman to speculate on such a matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, the witness indicated that the Spanish Battalion delegation visited Donja Mahala at the end of August, and I think the witness has said --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Nothing has to do with the other. He can elicit that, when did they visit, and he can give an answer. But he's asked to comment on a document which he never saw, he didn't draft. It's simply improper. It's trial advocacy 101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the Judges are concerned with are the contents of the document and here there is something that needs to be explained. According to this document, this is an appeal for help by the locals of Donja Mahala, and there were about 2.000 people there, or 2.900 people. In your memory, were there about 3.000 people living in Donja Mahala? Would you say that would be about correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, with a hundred people tolerance plus or minus. But there was about 3.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the document it says that Donja Mahala was an enclave, a part of the town where a majority of the population are Muslims without any protection, and so on and so forth. Would that correspond to the reality that you yourself experienced on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm really sorry to say, but nobody asks me how many dead and wounded I had. In the month of July of 1993, my command was decimated. I was the only one that survived. I was wounded and I -- still I had to make rounds of the lines. If you look at the number of dead only, there's nothing for me to say. Our combat readiness was reduced by 50 per cent excluding the civilians that arrived all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, in Donja Mahala, how many people were killed and how many were wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up to that time you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Approximately between 70 and a hundred approximately. I don't know the number of civilians, but the numbers can only be higher. It can't be any lower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. You're saying that UNPROFOR came to Donja Mahala. After their visit, did you feel a change? Was there more protection? Was protection better? Was there less shooting? Did the fire cease? Was there a -- fewer wounded and -- and killed, or did the situation continue the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two days later, the situation was same, and if -- if -- not only was it not better but it actually became worse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document and intervention is sought from the UNPROFOR, from the Red Cross. CNN TV is -- appealed to -- to come and visit. Did you see all these people? Did they come or did they not come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was not within my purview. This was under the authority of the MUP. As a military person I didn't have the right to contact with anybody. It was the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, did you see them yourself with your own two eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, please. I only saw the SpaBat APC. I didn't see anybody else, and I claim that with full responsibility. I know that there were Spaniards in a white APC, and I did not see anybody else. Again, I claim this with full responsibility. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: A follow-up question, and after that Mr. Praljak would like to say something. Concerning the question which was raised by the Presiding Judge, Judge Antonetti, he asked you if you saw some improvement or some movement by various organisations including ICRC or others. You mention now only the -- the Spanish Battalion. But previously, about five, 10 minutes ago, you mentioned that you witnessed or you were aware that certain assistance were delivered. Assistance what you mentioned, food, toiletries, et cetera. Now, what is your real position? Have you been aware of anything which was delivered there as assistance, as help in terms it of food and toiletries, et cetera, or you are only speaking about the -- about the Spanish Battalion's presence, which is, of course, another issue. So I believe now our question is if you had witnessed any improvement even only for a few days or weeks after this letter was originally sent. I hope you understand my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you are right, and I apologise. I did not understand you properly. The Spanish Battalion did come, indeed, and they brought aid in an APC. There was some improvement for a couple of days. They brought everything to -- to Donja Mahala local commune. I believe that there is a record to that effect, and this is the only thing that I can tell you. I had to pass through there. I couldn't go anywhere else because Donja Mahala is next to the road, and this was the only route that I could take to go anywhere. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] At the bottom of this document it says the original, illegible, handwritten, 2002, signed. We -- we don't have the illegible original. We don't have anything in handwriting. We don't have a date. Maybe it was signed in 2002, or written or something. And one really doesn't say how to comment such a document, save for the fact that war lends itself to a terrible propaganda by people who find themselves affected by war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Praljak has provided us a comment of the document and says that the contents are nothing but propaganda. What do you feel about that? How do you feel about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Chapeau Your Honours to both you and Mr. Praljak. I did not write this document. I did not see it at that time, but I swear by my life that whatever is contained in here I would die for it to prove that this is true. Sir, you have not seen a child starving. That's not propaganda. And when you see people who are dying, this is not propaganda. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] First of all, I apologise to Judge Antonetti. I didn't say that this is propaganda. I said that propaganda is a commonplace thing in any war, and the witness will obviously have something to say about this document, about people starving, being hungry, dying. But what it says here that this document is -- that it is illegible, that it is handwritten, that it doesn't have a date, that it was something in 2002, and that it was signed. Would that be a document that was written in 2002? Where is the original of this document? Who is the author of this document? And as for the reality of the life in Donja Mahala, this is a different issue and we'll learn about that in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, in theory when we introduce a document without a date you have to provide us with a criteria of reliability and tell us that the document arrives from this or that source, was provided by this person or something to that effect. This is to avoid objections and comments that have just been used and are a waste of time at the end of the day. What about this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the source of this document is -- it's -- we received this document from an ECMM officer. I don't know if I should call his name here out loud, but he's -- he's one of our witnesses, and he provide us this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Try and finish, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm almost finished, Your Honour. I must have maybe one or two questions about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, it says -- it talks about 2.900 persons and then it says both locals and refugees. Now, where did -- these refugees in Donja Mahala, where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: All the refugees who arrived in Donja Mahala arrived from the western part of Mostar, from Podhum, Zahum, Liska Street, Hit, Centar 2, the Avenue, Bonavac [phoen]. There are also people from Medjenje [phoen]. People who put lists together have the exact dates and numbers of people who had been expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And when did these refugees start to arrive in Donja Mahala?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first day of attack was the 9th of May, and I guarantee that on the day over a thousand refugees arrived in Donja Mahala, although we were not at all prepared. The shooting had already started. War started at 10 to 5.00. Shelling started, and the worst thing was the fact that these refugees were empty-handed. They didn't have anything on them, and this put a lot of pressure to bear on the small community of Mahala. Over the next two -- three or four months the number of population increased in Donja Mahala to 5.000. I can't be positive because I wasn't there. I only know that 2.000 people arrived at one point in -- during one month. This is where I was on duty. And there were so many people that we simply wasted all our food reserves within the first three months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question that might seem unimportant to you, but I have to ask that because it does present a problem. You are just -- you've just said that on the 9th of May there were a thousand displaced persons who arrived, and you say that in Donja Mahala at a certain moment there were up to 5.000 displaced persons, and you'll -- you're talking about the Napalm bombs, the tyres, and so on and so forth. One question that imposes itself: The individuals who were there, the refugees, could they not go somewhere else? Did they have to come to Donja Mahala? Was the entire zone encircled by the HVO? Is that why the people could not leave? Or was there a possibility to go elsewhere, and if that -- there was such a possibility, how come that these people didn't go anywhere? Or how come that they stayed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for putting this question. Three thousand people were locals, but suddenly the number increased to 5.000, which means that a total of 2.000 refugees had arrived. The first problem was the fact that the atomic shelter was full of refugees and people who performed their humanitarian work. The first question was, was there anybody in Bijelo Polje, Jablanica, Blagaj, on the left bank of the Neretva. Some people stayed with the families in Luka, in Tekija. A lot stayed in Mahala. We really wanted to try and -- and move these people from Mahala because there was a lot of pressure on us. The winter came, and I was given a task in December 1993 to take people to Jablanica. And that was the first time I was absent from Mahala for five days in the course of a whole year, because the war lasted nine months, but in Mahala it lasted 15 months, from April to June. During that March when we were taking people to Jablanica, my feet were frozen and all of my nails fell off. On Prenj, which is 2.100 metres high, on that side I counted at least 12 people who froze to death. When I returned from Jablanica on my way back from Jablanica, I again encountered a column of 500 people who were crossing the mountain to leave the town. So I can tell you who was it who crossed Prenj in the winter in December of 1993. I can tell you that a this was a heroic act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you haven't quite answered my question, because you're talking about the winter of 1993 when you climbed a mountain which was at an altitude of 2.100 metres, but my question is as follows: In the month of May, that is to say before the summer, Donja Mahala saw the arrival of thousands of people. So how come that these people were stuck there in Donja Mahala? Why didn't they go elsewhere, to some other place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. Those who could, went, and had somewhere to go, they left. But people didn't have any food. Everybody milled around the canteen. And to quote military doctrine, I prohibited one meal. I didn't let the meals be distributed to the soldiers but to the women and children and ailing elderly. There were a lot of people who were ailing, who were sick, and we endeavoured to transport them to the left bank. They had no medicines. So I can say with full responsibility that I did everything to have the people who could walk be taken to the opposite bank. That's what I wanted to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to avoid some misunderstandings, the witness so far hasn't referred to May, but he was speaking of the 9th of May, one particular day, the 9th of May, 1993, and he didn't speak of thousands of people who arrived in Donja Mahala from West Mostar, but he was talking about approximately 1.000 people who arrived from Western Mostar, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, I do respect you. However, Your Honours, on the 9th of May, in the morning, let me tell you, there were 1.260 people just that morning arriving in Donja Mahala. And if I'm wrong by one count, you can shoot me. One, two, three, even 500 people would come every day. I didn't count the people. I carried a rifle, gentlemen. I had to save my life and lives. And you can check out the lists. You have them all, and then you can check how many people poured in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, have you completed the examination-in-chief or do you need more time?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I did -- I do -- I am finished with my examination. The only thing I still want to do and I think we lost the Mostar map where the witness indicated where the tyres hit Donja Mahala. I would want to give that an IC number, but it seems that we've lost it. So I wonder if we could get the map back and he can make two markings again and we can have an IC number for that. And then I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be given Exhibit IC 420, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Am I correct that he will need to make a remarking of the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to give the map back to you. I don't know where the map has gone, but let's have it back and then you can have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 9517. So if we can pull that up on e-court, 9517.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that we are quite a bit overdue for the break. It may be convenient to have that done during the break and then we can avoid wasting time when we come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but -- yes. The witness might need to have a rest. Just answer -- or, rather, just follow the instructions given to you by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't need a rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Salcin, could you please mark the locations again where the tyres hit at Donja Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And if you could put your signature in the corner of this map, and if we could get an IC number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we have it. Mr. Registrar, what number was that? 420? 4-2-0. Is that it, Mr. Bos? We're going to take a break. It's 12.30, so we reconvene at 10 to 12.00. And we'll have 45 minutes, so think about who is going to start off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The cross-examination can start. I don't know who is going to kick off. Mr. Praljak. Let me remind you that the Defence has two and a half hours. So we're going to start the countdown as of now. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I have been given time from the Coric Defence and Pusic Defence as well as my own Defence and Mr. Stojic's Defence, 20 minutes or thereabouts, and I'll try and get through some matters calmly, because there seems to be a lot of chaos. Cross-examination by the Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's first decide on how we're going to proceed. When the Prosecutor asks you questions and Their Honours ask you questions, they let you provide them with various explanations. Now, I'd like to ask you, and that's your duty, to do your best to answer my questions briefly. My questions will be simple, as precise as possible, so please try and give me yes and no -- yes or no answers or say you don't know, I don't remember, I'm not aware of, that kind of thing. Brief. I don't need to listen to your explanations. Now, unless the Judges ask you to explain something, then try and be as brief as possible and avoid these long answers.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Praljak. I've understood you very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, let's try and clarify certain things straight away. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] May the witness be shown these two maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: On the first map we've already seen that aerial map of part of Hum, Stotina, and Mahala. And I'd like to ask you on that map to mark the positions that you had in Donja Mahala, the military positions. Is it true and correct that you were a member of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you were part of a battalion, the 41st Motorised Brigade, in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on this map, then, if that be the case, mark the HVO positions at Stotina, the line held by the HVO, and another line -- so that will be the first line. Line number 1 is the HVO line. Draw in the HVO positions at Stotina.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Leave the map the way it was. You needn't turn it round. Stotina is to the left.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And place a number 1 there, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now to the left of the bridge, the left bank of the Neretva, that was where the BH army positions were; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes, correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Draw them in, please, then -- or, rather, the line along the Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Well, I can't draw them around the Neretva River because that's not where they were. Mr. Praljak, this bridge had been destroyed, so there was no need for the BH army to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. Just put the area -- indicate the area under BH army control.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Praljak. The BH army was in South Camp, but I can't see that very well here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did the BH army control the left bank of the Neretva River up to the bridge that was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, go ahead and indicate then. Indicate that then.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: [Marks]. You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would you draw the line left of the bridge on the left bank where the position was, the BH army positions.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, it wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Then show us up until what place you were there. You were.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, there wasn't any guard duty. What was on that bank?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Praljak, but we were on the right bank because there was no need for us to be on the left bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Captain, do you know that shift duty and guard duty is not what it is in wartime? There are combat positions. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, look at Donja Mahala and indicate in Donja Mahala where your positions were.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Either draw a line or put Xs.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Where were you? Move the map so we can see it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Next.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And I assume you had positions further on.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes, we did, but I can't see them on the map. I understand, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now join the dotted lines up.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You were at Hum, weren't you, as well? Up at Hum?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Praljak. This is just -- these are just the scout positions where reconnoitering was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right. Then place the observation posts 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And the line, you can put a 4 for the line.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Given this line, in houses, basements, bunkers, is that where you had your positions?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: No, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: We just had points where we transferred the killed and wounded to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Are you claiming that the BH army and your particular unit that numbered 120 men opposite the HVO, facing the HVO, had points but no combat positions? Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, put your initials on that photograph and -- or, rather, leave the map there for another moment or two --

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: -- and mark the place where the tank was, the tank that you say targeted the old bridge that you saw.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I understand, sir. The first time or the second time?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You just saw the tank on the 8th of November, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Behind this house here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would you put a number there.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Which number?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Five, number 5.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And place your initials on the map as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I've already put them there. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] May the map be given an IC number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, an IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map will be given IC number 421, Your Honours. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] May we take a look at the next map now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: On this map you can see Stotina even better. It's a close-up. Would you mark the position of the tank that fired on the 8th of November, 1993, targeting the old bridge.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I understand, sir, but what time?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, I assume it was there the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I apologise, but, no, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right. Now, where did you see it? Mark the places where you saw it? Put a number 1 where you saw it first and a number 2 the next time you saw it.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: The next time it didn't shoot. It was just standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, do you see that there a he is a whole row of houses in front of that position? So tell me, from what position did you see the tank that you have indicated as being at number 2?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: From Hum.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You saw the tank there?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Not me but the scout.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Place your initials there, please, again.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So we can note that it wasn't you who saw the tank but the scout that saw the tank and conveyed that information to you.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I saw the tank on the first occasion, sir, but not the second occasion. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: That would be in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Now, may the witness be shown another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have an IC number, please, first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be given number IC 422, Your Honours. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: That is a sketch taken from a military map of the difference in altitude between the top of Hum the slopes going down towards Donja Mahala. Look at that sketch, please. The top of Hum is at 436, an altitude of 436 metres.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I apologise, but there's no need for people to whisper to you, into your ear. I can hear the person next to you whispering. There's no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Captain, you're here to answer my questions and not to tell me what to do.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Well, I can't hear very well in my left ear, but I can hear somebody else talking into a microphone and whispering to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: That's not your problem. I am asking clear questions, so please answer them. Can you see the sketch?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And is Hum at an altitude of 436 metres, the top of Hum? And the next area, is it at 379, at an altitude of 379 metres?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The Neretva River, is it just at an altitude of 60 metres, 60 metres above sea level?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: A little bit less.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How much less then?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: It's at about 50 but not 60 or 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right. Then put 50 metres then, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you reached the river Neretva, which is even lower that the point I marked, it's at 50 metres, Mr. Petkovic marked that, can you see with the naked eye, because the slope -- can you see the top of Hum, the peak?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right. Then draw a straight line as you would be seeing it with the naked eye. From the top of Hum draw a straight line. Not there. Not there. A diagonal line. You are standing at the Neretva River where we have the 50 metres, and then draw a straight lane, the angle of vision from that point to the top of Hum.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And tell me, how are you able to see the top of Hum hill from the Neretva River if there is a point in between which prevents and obstructs the view?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Sir, General --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just give me the answer.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: You can see the peak of mount Hum but it depends on which peak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: There is only one peak?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: I spent 20 years at Hum so tell me which peak. Is it Crvinje Pecine, Orlova [phoen] Pecine, Suplija [phoen] Pecine, Radobolja Pecine, they're all different caves, the red cave, et cetera. There's a tower up at the top. I can't see it that way, but the peak that I can see is one that I did see, not the one you're telling me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So looking from the Neretva River, you can see elevation 379, that feature; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you don't see the top of Hum, you see feature 379, elevation 379; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would you put your initials to the sketch so that we know that you cannot see the top of Hum hill from Neretva, which means that you can't see Donja Mahala from there either.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: [Marks]. From the top of Hum you can see Donja Mahala and Cekrk very well. And the sniper -- yes, you're right, General. You're right. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did we agree at the beginning that my questions would be very precise and that I ask you not to make comments about snipers and so on. My question is this: The elevation, the top of Hum which is at feature 436, It is 436 metres above sea level. Can you hear [as interpreted] it from Donja Mahala or not?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Not from half of Mahala but from the Cekrk and the Neretva River. There is an incline. So I can see it from one position but not from another.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: That is not possible logically.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: We'll go to the spot, the location and see who is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Never mind. Let's move on now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want a number? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes, a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, an IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be given number IC 423, Your Honours. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your unit, the one that was within the 2nd Battalion of the 41st [as interpreted] Motorised Brigade of the BH army, did it have its headquarters and command?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: During those war months and the conflict between the BH army and HVO, was a war diary or war log kept in your unit?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you ceased work or at the end of the war did you hand over this logbook, wartime diary or wartime logbook?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you tell us where your headquarters where in Gornja Mahala [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: The 1st Platoon was at Cekrk, the second was in Donja Mahala, Gojka Vukovica house, the third was in Spile at Dugalic's bakery, and the fourth was in the Ruza hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you regularly, per your establishment, send reports to your battalion and the 41st Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And in those reports, you describe the events, did you, who was killed, who was wounded and injured, the HVO actions? You wrote all this down regularly, all the combat operations?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: No, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: We shared spot for three sectors. The BH army did one, the MUP took over the civilians, and civilian protection did the rest because we weren't able to do the job ourselves. We had to sleep as well and have a rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In any case, there were three organisations, civilian protection, the MUP, and the BiH army, i.e., your unit, recorded certain events and developments. They wrote reports and they reported about the events.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did the Prosecution show you any of these documents? Did he place at your disposal to -- to talk about the events that you're describing for us here?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Know, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And now let's talk about two things. You've mentioned Ruza hotel.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN
utterances.text: Yes, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In 1992, when the Serbs were in Mostar, the Yugoslav Army and reservists, was the hotel torched by the army that I've just mentioned?
